title: The internet's down — or is it just DNS?
summary: Diagnose a 'the internet is down' call that's really a DNS failure: ping the IP, isolate name resolution, fix the resolver and prove the cause.
simplification: Simplified simulation: a real recursive lookup walks the root, TLD and authoritative servers, and DNS can use TCP for large answers. Tool output is scripted to mirror real nslookup, ping and ipconfig.

query.explain: Your PC asks its configured DNS resolver — here, the gateway — to turn the name shop.example.com into an IP address. DNS queries normally go out over UDP port 53.

guided.label: Guided
guided.intro: Watch a healthy DNS lookup turn the name shop.example.com into an IP address, one message at a time.
guided.debrief: That's name resolution: the PC asks its resolver, the resolver finds the authoritative answer, and the address comes back to be cached. When this breaks, you lose names but not necessarily the network itself.

practice.label: Practice
practice.intro: Same lookup — but predict each step before it happens.

lookup.q: The resolver has no cached answer. What does it do next?
options: Give up and tell the PC the site is down
Look the name up itself, asking other DNS servers on the PC's behalf
Ask the PC to try a different website
Broadcast the question to every device on the LAN
lookup.why: A recursive resolver does the work for you: it queries the root, TLD and authoritative servers until it has the answer, then caches it.

reply.q: The resolver now has 203.0.113.20. What happens last?
options: It returns the address to the PC, which caches it and connects
It installs the website on the PC
It changes the PC's IP address
It asks the gateway for permission
reply.why: DNS only maps names to addresses. Once the PC has the IP, it opens its own connection to the server — DNS is done.

practice.debrief: You can now narrate a DNS lookup end to end. Next, put it to work: diagnose a real outage in Challenge mode.

challenge.label: Challenge
challenge.intro: A user says "the internet is down" — but is it really? Investigate, fix it, then prove what the cause was.

opening.say: I can't open shop.example.com — the internet's down!
opening.log: Start: the PC can't load shop.example.com. Is the whole network down, or just name resolution?

hints: Don't trust "the internet is down." Can the PC reach anything by IP address? Try pinging the server's IP directly.
If the IP works but the name doesn't, the problem is name resolution — DNS — not connectivity.
Check which DNS server the PC is using (ipconfig), and whether it actually answers (nslookup).
Point the PC at a resolver you know works — the gateway at 192.168.1.1 — then look the name up again.

outcomes.finding: The PC's DNS server is now 192.168.1.1 (the gateway).
The PC's DNS server is set to 10.0.0.9, not the gateway.

outcomes.output:
Pinging 203.0.113.20 with 32 bytes of data:
Reply from 203.0.113.20: bytes=32 time=12ms TTL=118
Reply from 203.0.113.20: bytes=32 time=11ms TTL=118

Packets: Sent = 4, Received = 4, Lost = 0 (0% loss)
outcomes.finding: The web server answers on its IP, so the network path and the server are both fine.

outcomes.output:
Server:  gateway
Address: 192.168.1.1

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:    shop.example.com
Address: 203.0.113.20
outcomes.finding: With DNS set to 192.168.1.1, shop.example.com resolves to 203.0.113.20.

outcomes.output:
Name:    shop.example.com
Address: 203.0.113.20
(resolved from the hosts file, not DNS)
outcomes.finding: The name resolves — but from the hosts file, not DNS. Other names still fail.

outcomes.output:
Server:  UnKnown
Address: 10.0.0.9

DNS request timed out.
    timeout was 2 seconds.
*** Request to UnKnown timed out
*** Can't find shop.example.com: No response from server
outcomes.finding: The configured DNS server (10.0.0.9) isn't answering.

outcomes.output:
DNS server for the connection set to 192.168.1.1 (the gateway).
Run the lookup again to test it.
outcomes.finding: Pointed the PC at a working resolver (192.168.1.1).

outcomes.output:
Added to the hosts file:
203.0.113.20  shop.example.com
This one name now resolves locally, bypassing DNS entirely.
outcomes.finding: Added a hosts-file override for shop.example.com (one name only).

rootCause.q: It loads now. What was the actual cause of the outage?
options: The shop's web server was down
The PC was pointed at a DNS server that wasn't answering, so names couldn't be resolved
The network cable or gateway was faulty
A firewall was blocking the website
rootCause.why: Connectivity was fine all along — pinging the IP worked. Only name resolution failed, because the PC's configured DNS server (10.0.0.9) wasn't responding. Pointing it at a working resolver fixed it.
rootCause.evidenceQ: Which findings support that diagnosis? Tick the evidence, leave out what isn't.

evidence.text: Pinging the IP 203.0.113.20 directly got replies
evidence.why: This proves the network path and the server are fine, so the fault has to be name resolution, not connectivity.

evidence.text: nslookup to 10.0.0.9 timed out with no response
evidence.why: The configured DNS server simply wasn't answering — the direct cause of the failed lookups.

evidence.text: ipconfig showed the DNS server set to 10.0.0.9
evidence.why: This identifies the wrong/unreachable resolver the PC was relying on.

evidence.text: After switching DNS to 192.168.1.1, the name resolved
evidence.why: Confirms the fix addressed the real cause — useful, but not essential to the diagnosis.

evidence.text: The website returned a 500 server error
evidence.why: You never saw a server error. The browser couldn't even find the address — a different kind of failure.
Signal strength was never tested or implicated, and every ping to the IP succeeded.

challenge.debrief: Textbook troubleshooting: you tested connectivity (ping by IP), isolated the fault to DNS, found the misconfigured resolver, fixed it properly rather than papering over it with a hosts entry, and backed your diagnosis with evidence. "It's always DNS" — but only after you've proved it.
